x.A: Aurora provisioned instances cost money while running, and shutting them down each day requires a process to build and maintain.
x.B: A Service Catalog product that limits the size still launches Aurora instances that run and bill continuously.
x.C: Aurora Serverless scales capacity down to a minimum when idle, so developers pay mostly when they're active. A Service Catalog product launches databases in the cluster with the default capacity settings, so size and cost stay limited.
x.D: Terminating idle databases after Trusted Advisor flags them is a manual, reactive process, and the developers would lose their databases.

x.A: Copying assets from the newest instance and writing only to it is complex, creates a single point of failure, and the instances wouldn't share up-to-date content in real time.
x.B: EFS is a shared file system that all instances across AZs mount, so every instance sees changes immediately, with the least lag.
x.C: Syncing from S3 once an hour means up to an hour of lag, and files are duplicated on each instance.
x.D: An EBS snapshot restored for each instance gives each its own copy, so updates aren't shared.

x.A: GuardDuty detects suspicious behavior in the AWS environment, EventBridge filters its findings, and a Lambda function can automatically update AWS WAF rules to respond, such as blocking malicious IP addresses.
x.B: Firewall Manager manages firewall policies and doesn't do threat detection or produce findings in that way.
x.C: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't detect suspicious behavior or update WAF rules.
x.D: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 and doesn't detect threats to the web application.

x.A: A database user name and password passed as template parameters are static credentials, which the company doesn't want to maintain.
x.B: Credentials in Parameter Store are still static credentials that need to be rotated and retrieved.
x.C: IAM database authentication lets the instances authenticate with a short-lived token through an IAM role, so there are no static database credentials to maintain.
x.D: IAM users can't be associated with EC2 instances. Instances use IAM roles.

x.A: CloudFront can't use private certificates from ACM Private CA for a public distribution, and private CA certificates cost extra.
x.B: CloudFront requires the certificate to be in us-east-1, and private certificates aren't trusted by public browsers.
x.C: A public certificate from ACM in us-east-1 is free and CloudFront can use it for the custom domain name, so it doesn't add cost.
x.D: CloudFront requires the ACM certificate to be in us-east-1, so a certificate in us-west-1 can't be used.

x.A: Migrating data to a new public bucket exposes the data to everyone, not only the consultant, and it takes work.
x.B: Making the whole bucket public exposes all the operations data, not just the report.
x.C: An IAM user with access keys means long-term credentials and manual revocation after 7 days.
x.D: A presigned URL for the report grants time-limited access to only that object, and expires automatically after 7 days. It's the most efficient and secure way.

x.A: A cluster placement group packs instances close together in one AZ, giving the low-latency, high-throughput network performance that tightly coupled HPC needs.
x.B: Dedicated Instance tenancy gives hardware isolation and doesn't improve network performance between nodes.
x.C: Spot Instances reduce cost and don't affect network performance, and they can be interrupted.
x.D: A Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity and has nothing to do with network performance.

x.A: Two connections from only the primary data center leave the secondary data center out, so the failure of the primary site would cut off connectivity.
x.B: A single connection from each data center to one location on the same device is a single point of failure at the location and device.
x.C: Two connections from each data center, ending at two different Direct Connect locations on separate devices, remove single points of failure at the connection, device, location, and data center, giving maximum resiliency.
x.D: One connection from each data center at a single location is still a single point of failure if that location fails.

x.A: In an organization, the Trusted Advisor recommendations in the management account give an organization-wide view, so the finance team can see checks across the member accounts in one place.
x.B: Checking each member account separately takes more time, and the finance team has access to the management account that gives the consolidated view.
x.C: The instances are On-Demand with high utilization for a long time, so the RDS Reserved Instance Optimization check can show savings by buying reservations.
x.D: The Idle DB Instances check finds instances with no connections, and these instances have high utilization, so it doesn't apply.
x.E: Compute optimization checks apply to EC2, not to RDS databases.

x.A: A gateway endpoint for S3 sends traffic to S3 on the AWS network and has no hourly or data processing charges, so it minimizes data transfer costs for large files. The route table entry sends S3 traffic to it.
x.B: A single NAT gateway charges per GB processed and per hour, and cross-AZ traffic adds charges. It's costly for large files.
x.C: An interface endpoint for S3 has hourly and per-GB charges, so it costs more than the free gateway endpoint, and you don't add route table entries for it.
x.D: NAT gateways in every AZ add hourly charges and data processing charges, so it costs more.

x.A: RDS for MySQL with Provisioned IOPS storage handles high write volumes with consistent performance, and monitoring write metrics lets you adjust the provisioned IOPS as needed.
x.B: A cache helps reads, not heavy writes, and General Purpose SSD may not sustain the write load.
x.C: DocumentDB is a document database, so it isn't compatible with a MySQL application.
x.D: EFS is a file system and isn't a database to store the application's data.

x.A: Client-side encryption isn't a bucket setting with S3 managed keys. S3 managed keys are used for server-side encryption.
x.B: Server-side encryption encrypts the data after S3 receives it, so third parties could access the data before it's encrypted and sent.
x.C: Dual-layer server-side encryption still happens in AWS after the data is sent, so data isn't protected before it leaves the application.
x.D: Client-side encryption in the application with a KMS key encrypts the files before they leave the application, so third parties can't access the plaintext data on its way to S3.

x.A: A Lambda function to create snapshots is custom code to build and maintain, when automated backups already exist.
x.B: Automated backups already take a daily backup. Changing the retention period from the default (7 days) to 30 days keeps them for 30 days with just one setting.
x.C: Maintenance Windows is for patching, and it isn't how backup retention is changed.
x.D: Daily manual snapshots with the CLI are manual work and aren't needed.

x.A: A second cluster with a copy job needs a separate sync process and costs more, and replication could lag.
x.B: DAX works only with DynamoDB, not with Aurora.
x.C: An Aurora read replica in the same cluster handles read-only queries through the reader endpoint, so reads don't slow down writes on the cluster endpoint. It's cost-effective.
x.D: Redshift is a data warehouse, and copying data to it adds cost, complexity, and lag.

x.A: Kinesis Data Firehose ingests streaming data in near real time and scales automatically, so it's serverless ingestion.
x.B: Lambda has a 15 minute maximum run time, so it can't run a 30 minute job.
x.C: DMS migrates databases and isn't a streaming ingestion service.
x.D: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group means managing servers, so it isn't serverless.
x.E: ECS on Fargate runs containers without servers, with no 15 minute limit, so it can handle the 30 minute job and scale.

x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 with a route in the route table sends the traffic over the AWS network, so the data never uses the public internet.
x.B: An NLB can't have an S3 bucket as a target.
x.C: S3 buckets can't be deployed inside a VPC, because S3 is a Regional service.
x.D: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS, and doesn't connect a VPC to an S3 endpoint.

x.A: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not EBS cost optimization.
x.B: Systems Manager reports on instance configuration and compliance, not volume cost savings.
x.C: CloudWatch metrics show utilization but don't generate recommendations with estimated monthly savings.
x.D: Compute Optimizer analyzes EBS volume configuration and utilization and recommends optimizations, including estimated monthly savings.

x.A: The text of this option is missing in the source material, so it can't be evaluated here.
x.B: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide visibility across Regions and accounts with metrics and recommendations, including which buckets don't have versioning enabled.
x.C: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 shows buckets with public or cross-account access, not their versioning status.
x.D: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests across buckets in different Regions and doesn't report on versioning.

x.A: An SQS FIFO queue processes each order exactly once and in order, buffers surges so customers aren't affected, and a Lambda function consumes and processes the orders.
x.B: An SNS standard topic delivers at least once and can send duplicates, and it doesn't buffer during surges.
x.C: AppFlow transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS services and isn't an order processing queue.
x.D: X-Ray traces requests for debugging and doesn't process orders, and CloudWatch isn't a queue to pull orders from.

x.A: Policies by themselves can't give access across accounts without a role to assume, and creating them in each account for individual developers doesn't scale.
x.B: A role in the Development account can't grant access to resources in the Production account. The role must be in the account that owns the resources.
x.C: A role in the Production account with a trust policy for the Development account lets developers assume it for access. For the beta phase, more developers can be given permission to assume the role.
x.D: A group can't be a principal in a trust policy, and the trust policy has to specify the Development account, not Production.

x.A: Cognito provides scalable, serverless authentication, Lambda@Edge authorizes requests at CloudFront edge locations with low latency, and CloudFront serves the application globally. It scales as the user base grows.
x.B: Directory Service for Microsoft AD isn't serverless and costs more for a small user base, and an ALB doesn't serve content globally.
x.C: Lambda in a single Region adds login latency for global users, and Transfer Acceleration doesn't serve a web application globally.
x.D: Directory Service isn't serverless, and Elastic Beanstalk doesn't serve content globally.

x.A: IAM policies must be updated and applied to all users in every account, which is a lot of work and can be bypassed by admins.
x.B: Resource Access Manager shares resources and can't prevent the launch of instance types.
x.C: An IAM role in each account that denies large instances doesn't restrict developers who aren't using the role, and it must be created in every account.
x.D: An SCP applied through Organizations denies launching large instance types across all accounts from one place, which needs the least operational work.

x.A: Patch Manager handles inventory and patching, but Security Hub aggregates findings and isn't the vulnerability scanner that produces a summary of each instance's common vulnerabilities.
x.B: Patch Manager automates OS patching and inventory for Windows and Linux instances, and Inspector scans the instances for vulnerabilities and can produce monthly reports.
x.C: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS and Config doesn't install patches.
x.D: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't summarize vulnerabilities, and Config doesn't automate patch installations.

x.A: A running Auto Scaling group and ELB in the DR Region, a DynamoDB global table, and DNS failover provides the least downtime because the environment is already running and data is replicated.
x.B: Building everything with CloudFormation when needed takes time to deploy and the DynamoDB data wouldn't be there, so downtime is longer.
x.C: Launching the EC2 instances and ELB from a template when needed takes time, so downtime is longer than having them ready.
x.D: A CloudWatch alarm with a 10 minute evaluation period delays the failover, and updating Route 53 with Lambda is more custom than DNS failover.

x.A: A NAT gateway sends traffic through the internet gateway, so it travels over the public internet, and it adds hourly and data charges.
x.B: Storage Gateway is a hybrid storage service and isn't meant for EC2 instances to reach S3 privately, and it adds cost.
x.C: An S3 interface endpoint works privately, but it has hourly and data processing charges.
x.D: An S3 gateway endpoint keeps traffic on the AWS network at no additional cost, so it's the most cost-effective private option.
